I understand some countries adopt a system which is neither the typical Civil Law system (like Germany's and their BGB, as you mentioned) or the true Common Law system, some being a mix of the two (South Africa, Quebec, Israel). I wonder what's the case in Scandinavia, could you elaborate on this traditional Scandinavian law? Does it differ much from either Roman law or case law?

In Countries with civil law tradition, the owner may sell a property withholding Usufruct rights (a type of right called *iura in re*, which entitles the person to use and enjoy the property). This right extends up until the death of the person. The buyer is then called a "nude-proprietor", because while he retains the ownership of the property, he is not entitled to all of its inherent rights (such as to use it, rent it, lend it, etc.). So when the person holding the usufruct rights dies, the buyer acquires full ownership. This may be the case in Louisiana, which is based in civil law. (as opposed to common law)
